summary: Older-school MAOI antidepressant for major depression when other treatments haven’t worked. Can be effective, but it comes with strict food/drug rules and real safety risks (hypertensive crisis, serotonin syndrome).
description: Marplan is an MAOI antidepressant used for major depressive disorder when other antidepressants haven’t helped enough. It can take a few weeks to kick in, and it requires a tyramine-restricted diet plus serious caution with other meds (especially SSRIs/SNRIs, stimulants, dextromethorphan, and certain pain meds). Biggest headline risks: hypertensive crisis, serotonin syndrome, orthostatic hypotension, and the standard antidepressant suicidality boxed warning in younger patients. This is a specialist-level medication—worth it for the right person, not casual.
patient_summary: Marplan is a MAOI antidepressant used for major depression when other meds haven’t worked. It takes weeks to build benefit and requires strict food/drug restrictions to avoid dangerous blood pressure spikes or serotonin syndrome. It can cause dizziness, headaches, sleep disruption, and blood pressure drops when standing. Like other antidepressants, it carries a boxed warning for increased suicidal thoughts/behavior in some younger people early in treatment—close monitoring matters.

primary.context: Used for unipolar major depression as an alternative option when more standard antidepressants haven’t helped enough or weren’t tolerated. Because MAOIs have high interaction risk, they’re typically reserved for treatment-resistant cases and managed carefully.

off_label.context: Often considered when multiple adequate antidepressant trials have failed. This is a common real-world use-case for MAOIs, but it requires strict diet/medication rules and close monitoring.

therapeutic_response.display: Depression: initial effects may appear within 1–2 weeks

common_adverse_effects.notes: This can feel like lightheadedness or wobbliness, especially when standing up. Hydration, slow position changes, and checking blood pressure can help.
Headaches can occur, but a sudden severe headache with sweating, neck stiffness, or nausea/vomiting is a red flag for hypertensive crisis—don’t ignore that.
Hydration, fiber, and gentle stool softeners (when appropriate and cleared by a clinician) can help.
Sugar-free gum, hydration, and oral care matter—dry mouth can sneak up on your teeth and gums.
Sometimes improves over time. If it’s persistent, dose timing and split dosing can help.
This can be insomnia or fragmented sleep. If sleep is getting worse, talk with your prescriber early rather than suffering in silence.
If you feel overly sedated, avoid driving and risky tasks until you know your baseline.
Lightheadedness and fainting risk increase with dehydration, hot showers, alcohol, and certain medications.

serious_risks.risk: Hypertensive crisis (sometimes fatal): severe headache, sweating, nausea/vomiting, stiff/sore neck, photophobia, dangerously high blood pressure. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Serotonin syndrome: agitation/confusion, fever, sweating, diarrhea, tremor, muscle rigidity, fast heart rate, high blood pressure. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Seizures: risk may increase in susceptible patients; severe withdrawal/discontinuation can also involve seizures. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Hepatotoxicity: abnormal liver function tests, jaundice; risk is higher with pre-existing liver disease. Stop and evaluate urgently if jaundice or severe right-upper-abdominal pain occurs.
Severe mood/behavior change: suicidal ideation/tendencies, abrupt worsening depression, new agitation/hostility/impulsivity, mania/hypomania. Urgent clinical evaluation needed.

safety.black_box_warning: Suicidality and antidepressant drugs: Antidepressants increased the risk (vs placebo) of suicidal thinking and behavior in short-term studies in children, adolescents, and young adults with MDD and other psychiatric disorders. Closely monitor patients of all ages for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual behavior changes—especially in the first 1–2 months and during dose changes. Advise families/caregivers to observe closely and communicate with the prescriber. Marplan is not approved for use in pediatric patients.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to isocarboxazid or any component of the formulation
History of headache (per labeling/precautions context due to hypertensive crisis risk)
History of hepatic disease or abnormal liver function tests
Concurrent use with contraindicated medications or foods high in tyramine (risk of hypertensive crisis) and serotonergic agents (risk of serotonin syndrome)

precautions: Hypertensive crisis: Sometimes fatal blood pressure spikes can occur, especially with tyramine-rich foods or interacting meds. Symptoms can include severe headache, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness/soreness, photophobia, sweating, and dangerously high blood pressure.
Serotonin syndrome: Can occur if combined with serotonergic medications (SSRIs/SNRIs, certain TCAs, linezolid, dextromethorphan, some opioids, and others). This can be life-threatening.
Orthostatic hypotension and syncope: Standing-related dizziness/fainting can happen—risk rises with dehydration, certain BP meds, and older age.
Mania/hypomania risk: Antidepressants can precipitate mania/hypomania in bipolar disorder. Screen for bipolar history before starting; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar depression.
Seizure threshold: Can lower seizure threshold; use caution in seizure risk states (history of seizures, head trauma, alcohol use disorder, interacting meds).
Liver and kidney risk: Contraindicated with hepatic disease/abnormal LFTs and contraindicated in severe renal impairment.

Surgery/anesthesia: Certain anesthetic and pain medication combinations are dangerous. Manufacturer guidance includes stopping prior to elective surgery; if continued, anesthesia must be MAOI-safe (no meperidine; avoid indirect-acting adrenergic agents).
Discontinuation syndrome: Abrupt stopping can cause severe neuropsychiatric symptoms (agitation, delirium, insomnia, irritability, myoclonic jerks, seizures, hallucinations).

interactions.interactant: Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheeses, cured/aged meats, tap/draft beer, fermented soy products, sauerkraut, spoiled/improperly stored foods)
interactions.action: Strict avoidance. Food freshness/storage matters because tyramine rises as foods age or spoil. If severe headache, sweating, chest pain, stiff neck, or severe nausea/vomiting occurs—go to urgent care/ER.

interactions.mechanism: High risk of serotonin syndrome and other severe reactions.
interactions.action: Do not combine. Washout rules matter: typically wait at least 14 days between stopping most antidepressants and starting isocarboxazid; wait 5 weeks after fluoxetine before starting isocarboxazid; and wait at least 7–14 days after stopping isocarboxazid before starting another antidepressant (longer depending on the agent).

interactions.mechanism: Excess MAOI effect and severe adverse reactions (hypertensive crisis, serotonin syndrome).
interactions.action: Avoid overlap. Follow washout periods before switching.

interactions.interactant: Sympathomimetics and stimulants (amphetamines, cocaine, pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine and related agents)
interactions.mechanism: Hypertensive crisis, severe blood pressure spikes, arrhythmias.
interactions.action: Avoid. This includes many decongestants and “energy” products.

interactions.mechanism: Serotonin syndrome and severe CNS reactions.

interactions.interactant: Meperidine and certain opioids / CNS depressants (including alcohol)
interactions.mechanism: Severe CNS depression, dangerous interactions, and potentially life-threatening reactions.
interactions.action: Avoid. If pain control or anesthesia is needed, the treating team must use an MAOI-safe plan.
Do not combine. Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting bupropion (or vice versa per switching guidance).
Do not combine. Allow at least 10 days between stopping isocarboxazid and starting buspirone per guidance.
Avoid certain combinations per labeling and monitor blood pressure closely if any BP-lowering agents are necessary.

interactions.mechanism: Can contribute to adverse reactions and blood pressure instability.
interactions.action: Avoid excessive caffeine and monitor how your body responds.

interactions.interactant: General and spinal anesthesia; local vasoconstrictors
interactions.mechanism: Potential exaggerated hypotension or severe reactions depending on agents used.
interactions.action: Surgeon/anesthesiologist must be informed. Elective surgery planning may require stopping medication ahead of time or using an MAOI-safe anesthetic approach.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Mood and suicidality: especially early in treatment (first 1–2 months) and during dose changes. Monitor for clinical worsening, suicidal ideation, agitation, hostility, impulsivity, insomnia, and unusual behavior changes.
Blood pressure and heart rate: baseline and ongoing. Monitor for hypertensive crisis symptoms and orthostatic hypotension (standing BP checks can be useful).
Diet adherence and medication reconciliation: review food restrictions and all meds/supplements at every visit (including OTC cold meds and stimulants).
Renal function: baseline and periodic, especially if any impairment is present.
Liver function tests: baseline and periodic; stop and evaluate if jaundice or significant LFT abnormalities occur.
Sleep and activation: insomnia, agitation, hyperactive behavior, and anxiety can worsen in some patients—track and adjust plan early.
Mania/hypomania screening: monitor for mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, risky behavior, pressured speech, and irritability—especially if bipolar risk factors exist.
Seizure risk: monitor patients with seizure history or risk factors and avoid combinations that lower seizure threshold.

special_populations.pregnancy: Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted (per provided notes). If pregnant while taking antidepressants, consider enrolling in the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants (NPRAD). Because MAOIs require strict interaction management and can cause significant cardiovascular effects, many clinicians prefer alternative antidepressants with more pregnancy safety data when possible.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known if isocarboxazid is present in breast milk. Manufacturer guidance recommends use in nursing only if clearly needed. If breastfeeding, this should be a deliberate, specialist-level risk/benefit discussion with close infant monitoring if used.
special_populations.pediatric: Not approved for use in pediatric patients (per boxed warning language provided). If a young patient is being considered for an MAOI at all, this should be managed by a specialist with very close monitoring and clear rationale.
special_populations.geriatric: Refer to adult dosing (per provided notes). In real-world practice, older adults may be more vulnerable to orthostatic hypotension, falls, and medication interactions—so dosing and titration should be cautious, with close blood pressure monitoring.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment. Use with caution in mild-to-moderate impairment to reduce risk of accumulation and adverse effects.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Contraindicated in patients with a history of liver disease or abnormal liver function tests.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral administration; clinical effect is delayed compared with dose timing
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food interactions are clinically critical: tyramine-containing foods can trigger hypertensive crisis. Freshness/spoilage matters because tyramine rises as foods age or are improperly stored.

dosing.titration: Marplan dosing is typically split into multiple doses per day and titrated upward based on response and tolerability. Antidepressant benefit can take weeks—so dose changes should be deliberate, not chaotic.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Stopping Marplan abruptly (or with an overly fast taper) can trigger a discontinuation syndrome—sometimes intense—with agitation, delirium/confusion, insomnia, irritability, mood crash, myoclonic jerks, and in severe cases seizures. Tapering also gives you a chance to catch returning depression early rather than being blindsided.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Marplan is used for major depressive disorder (unipolar depression), usually when other antidepressants haven’t worked well enough or weren’t tolerated. It’s not a first-choice antidepressant because the interaction and diet rules are intense—but for the right person, it can be a legitimate difference-maker.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Persistent depression, low motivation, impaired functioning, and mood symptoms that haven’t responded to more typical options
Alternative antidepressant option: Often considered after multiple antidepressant trials have failed or caused intolerable side effects
Specialist-managed depression care: Best handled with careful education, medication reconciliation, and diet planning

sections.intro: This one has a very specific vibe: it’s not usually an instant “I feel it in an hour” med. It’s more like a slow shift—plus you’ll notice the body stuff (blood pressure, dizziness) before you notice the mood lift. Common experiences look like this:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Marplan is not a “take it today, feel it tonight” antidepressant. Expect a gradual mood shift over weeks—not hours.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: You may notice early changes (slightly less heaviness, fewer spirals, marginally better energy)
3–6 weeks: Typical window for clearer antidepressant benefit
~6 weeks: If there’s no meaningful response at an adequate dose, further dose pushes are less likely to suddenly work
After stopping: MAOI effects can linger, which is why washout periods are required before switching to many other antidepressants

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Marplan can be effective for major depression, especially in people who haven’t had enough benefit from more standard antidepressants. The trade-off is the complexity: diet restrictions, dangerous interactions, and a need for close monitoring. If you’re going to use an MAOI, you’re doing it on purpose—and you’re doing it carefully.
sections.clinical_details: MAOIs are typically positioned as later-line antidepressants because of interaction risks and the possibility of hypertensive crisis or serotonin syndrome. When selected thoughtfully (and paired with strict education and monitoring), they can provide meaningful symptom improvement for some patients with persistent depression.

No “I’ll just try a little” with tyramine foods. Avoid aged cheeses, cured/aged meats, tap/draft beer, certain fermented soy products, sauerkraut, and other high-tyramine items. Freshness and storage matter.
Know the emergency symptoms: severe headache, chest pain, stiff neck, sweating, palpitations, confusion, high fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, or severe agitation—seek urgent care/ER.
Monitor mood closely early in treatment. If suicidal thoughts intensify, or behavior becomes unusually agitated/impulsive, contact your prescriber urgently.
Stand up slowly, hydrate, and report fainting, falls, or severe dizziness.

sections.intro: MAOI interactions are not “minor.” Some combinations can be fatal. The safest approach is: assume an interaction until proven otherwise and confirm with a pharmacist/clinician before adding anything new.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stopping Marplan abruptly (or with an overly fast taper) can trigger a discontinuation syndrome—sometimes intense—with agitation, delirium/confusion, insomnia, irritability, mood crash, myoclonic jerks, and in severe cases seizures. Tapering also gives you a chance to catch returning depression early rather than being blindsided.
key_points: If treatment has lasted ≥4 weeks: taper gradually over ~2–4 weeks to reduce withdrawal symptoms and watch for relapse.
If treatment has lasted 2–3 weeks: taper over ~1–2 weeks may be reasonable.
<2 weeks of treatment: tapering may not be necessary for everyone, but don’t assume—some people are sensitive.
More conservative tapers may be needed with MAOIs, higher doses, longer duration, or prior history of discontinuation symptoms.
If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable: return to the previously tolerated dose and taper more slowly.
Long-term treatment (>6 months): some patients benefit from very slow tapers (sometimes >3 months), especially if they’ve had discontinuation syndrome before.

Switching washouts matter: allow time between stopping/starting other antidepressants and Marplan to prevent serotonin syndrome or hypertensive reactions (for example, 14 days for most antidepressants; 5 weeks after fluoxetine before starting Marplan; and at least 7–14 days after stopping Marplan before starting another antidepressant).

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Marplan dosing is typically split into multiple doses per day and titrated upward based on response and tolerability. Antidepressant benefit can take weeks—so dose changes should be deliberate, not chaotic.

adult.depression_titration_week1: Increase total daily dose by 10 mg increments every 2 to 4 days as tolerated, up to 40 mg/day by the end of week 1 (in 2 to 4 divided doses per day)
adult.depression_titration_after_week1: After week 1, may increase by up to 20 mg/week based on response and tolerability
adult.depression_max: 60 mg/day PO in 2 to 4 divided doses
adult.response_window: May take 3 to 6 weeks to see meaningful effects; if no response within ~6 weeks at an adequate dose, further titration is less likely to help
adult.dose_caution: Use caution with doses >40 mg/day because clinical experience is limited

sections.simple_explanation: This is a slower-build antidepressant. You start at a low dose, step up carefully, and give it time to work. Meanwhile, the safety rules (food and medication interactions) matter from day one.

sections.text: Marplan has limited pregnancy and breastfeeding data, and it carries serious interaction and blood pressure risks. In special populations, the risk-benefit calculation needs to be explicit—not assumed.

Because MAOIs require strict interaction management and can cause significant cardiovascular effects, many clinicians prefer alternative antidepressants with more pregnancy safety data when possible.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Marplan is available as an oral tablet. Because dosing is titrated and split across the day, having a consistent formulation matters for stable dosing and monitoring.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Marplan works by inhibiting monoamine oxidase (MAO), the enzyme that breaks down neurotransmitters like serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. By blocking MAO, levels of these neurotransmitters increase over time, which can improve depressive symptoms. The flip side is that MAO also interacts with dietary amines (like tyramine) and many medications—so the interaction list is long and the safety rules are strict.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Marplan is typically a later-line antidepressant—meaning it’s usually considered after first-line and second-line options (like SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, mirtazapine, psychotherapy, and augmentation strategies) haven’t delivered enough benefit. The reason isn’t that it “doesn’t work”—it’s that MAOIs demand real structure: strict diet rules, medication interaction vigilance, and close monitoring for blood pressure and dangerous syndromes. When used intentionally (and correctly), it can be a powerful tool for the right depression picture.

faqs.a: Marplan (isocarboxazid) is used to treat major depressive disorder (unipolar depression). It’s typically considered when more common antidepressants haven’t helped enough, because MAOIs require strict food and medication restrictions to prevent dangerous reactions.

faqs.q: How long does Marplan take to work?
faqs.a: You may notice early changes within 1–2 weeks, but the stronger antidepressant benefit usually builds over 3–6 weeks. If there’s no meaningful improvement by about 6 weeks at an adequate dose, further dose increases are less likely to help.

faqs.q: Why does Marplan require a special diet?
faqs.a: Marplan is an MAOI, and MAOIs can react with tyramine found in certain aged/fermented foods. That interaction can trigger a hypertensive crisis—a sudden, dangerous spike in blood pressure. Avoiding high-tyramine foods and being careful about food freshness/storage is part of the safety plan.

faqs.q: What foods should I avoid on Marplan?
faqs.a: Avoid tyramine-heavy foods like aged/matured cheeses, air-dried or cured meats (including sausages and salamis), tap/draft beers, certain fermented soy products/condiments, sauerkraut, and foods that are spoiled or improperly stored. When in doubt, treat it as a “no” until you confirm it’s safe.

faqs.q: What medications are dangerous with Marplan?
faqs.a: Many. The biggest danger zones are SSRIs/SNRIs and other serotonergic meds (serotonin syndrome risk), stimulants and decongestants like pseudoephedrine/phenylephrine (hypertensive crisis risk), dextromethorphan (serotonin syndrome risk), and certain pain/anesthesia meds like meperidine. Always check with a pharmacist/clinician before adding anything—even OTC cold meds.

faqs.q: How do switching washout periods work with Marplan?
faqs.a: Washouts are required to prevent serotonin syndrome and other severe reactions. Common guidance: wait about 14 days between stopping most antidepressants (without long-lasting metabolites) and starting Marplan; wait 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting Marplan; and wait at least 7–14 days after stopping Marplan before starting another antidepressant. Specific cases can vary, so the prescriber should map this out clearly.

faqs.q: Does Marplan have a boxed warning?
faqs.a: Yes. Like other antidepressants, it carries the boxed warning about increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies. The key clinical action is close monitoring—especially in the first 1–2 months and during dose changes—and involving family/caregivers when appropriate.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of Marplan?
faqs.a: The most commonly reported side effects include dizziness and headache. Other common effects include dry mouth, constipation, nausea, sleep disturbance, drowsiness, tremor, and orthostatic hypotension (lightheadedness when standing).

faqs.q: What is a hypertensive crisis and what does it feel like?
faqs.a: A hypertensive crisis is a sudden, dangerous rise in blood pressure that can happen with tyramine foods or interacting medications while on an MAOI. Warning signs can include a sudden severe headache, sweating, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness/soreness, photophobia, palpitations, and very high blood pressure. This is an emergency—seek urgent care/ER.

Yes—especially if combined with serotonergic medications (like SSRIs/SNRIs), dextromethorphan, and other interacting agents. Symptoms can include agitation/confusion, fever, sweating, diarrhea, tremor, muscle rigidity, fast heart rate, and high blood pressure. This is a medical emergency.

faqs.q: How do I stop Marplan safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for at least 4 weeks, a gradual taper over about 2–4 weeks is commonly recommended to reduce discontinuation symptoms and watch for relapse. MAOIs can have more intense discontinuation syndromes, so some people need slower tapers—especially at higher doses or longer durations. If withdrawal symptoms are severe, the usual move is to return to the prior dose and taper more slowly.
